item.title: “Monks, what is Right Effort? Monks, here a monk awakens desire for the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome states; he makes an effort, arouses energy,…
item.description:
“Monks, what is Right Effort? Monks, here a monk awakens desire for the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome states; he makes an effort, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives. He awakens desire for the abandoning of arisen evil, unwholesome states; he makes an effort, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives. He awakens desire for the arising of unarisen wholesome states; he makes an effort, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives. He awakens desire for the continuance, non-disappearance, strengthening, increase, and fulfillment of arisen wholesome states; he makes an effort, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives. This, monks, is called Right Effort.”

From: Dīgha Nikāya 22 – Mahāsatipaṭṭhānasutta

item.title: “And for what benefit, monks, should a monk dwell with the perception of disgust toward the non-disgusting? ‘May greed not arise in me toward agreeable…
item.description:
“And for what benefit, monks, should a monk dwell with the perception of disgust toward the non-disgusting? ‘May greed not arise in me toward agreeable states.’ For this benefit, monks, a monk should dwell with the perception of disgust toward the non-disgusting. And for what benefit, monks, should a monk dwell with the perception of non-disgust toward the disgusting? ‘May hatred not arise in me toward states that provoke hatred.’ For this benefit, a monk should dwell with the perception of non-disgust toward the disgusting. And for what benefit should a monk, abandoning both the non-disgusting and the disgusting, dwell equanimously, mindful and clearly comprehending? ‘May greed not arise in me toward agreeable states, wherever, however; may hatred not arise in me toward states that provoke hatred, wherever, however; may delusion not arise in me toward states that provoke delusion, wherever, however.’ For this benefit, monks, a monk, abandoning both the non-disgusting and the disgusting, dwells equanimously, mindful and clearly comprehending.”

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.144

item.title: “Monks, suppose there is a bronze cup of drinking water that has color, smell, and taste, and that drinking water is mixed with poison. Then…
item.description:
“Monks, suppose there is a bronze cup of drinking water that has color, smell, and taste, and that drinking water is mixed with poison. Then a man comes who desires to live, not to die, who desires happiness and loathes suffering. Someone says to him: ‘Good man, this bronze cup of drinking water has color, smell, and taste, and it is mixed with poison. If you wish, drink it. While drinking, you will delight in its color, smell, and taste. After drinking, you may meet death or deadly suffering.’ That man might drink it without reflection, without refusal. While drinking, he delights in its color, smell, and taste. After drinking, he meets death or deadly suffering. Monks, I say that this course of practice is like that simile — namely, a course of practice that is pleasant in the present but has painful results in the future.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 46 – Mahādhammasamādānasutta

item.title: Those who are intoxicated with states, Bewildered and confused, Led astray into wrong courses, Wandering amidst various views — They sleep on and on, They…
item.description:
Those who are intoxicated with states,
Bewildered and confused,
Led astray into wrong courses,
Wandering amidst various views —
They sleep on and on,
They do not wake up.
Now indeed the time has come
For them to awaken.

(The Blessed One):
Those who are not intoxicated with states,
Not bewildered or confused,
Not led astray into wrong courses,
Wandering amidst various views —
They have attained perfect enlightenment,
They have fully understood.
On the uneven path,
They walk evenly.

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.8
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: Elder Nitaka: The mind is like a rock, Standing firm, unmoved. Toward agreeable things, The mind has no desire. Toward things that disturb, The mind…
item.description:
Elder Nitaka:

The mind is like a rock,
Standing firm, unmoved.
Toward agreeable things,
The mind has no desire.
Toward things that disturb,
The mind is not disturbed.
One whose mind is thus developed —
From where can suffering come?

My mind is like a rock,
Standing firm, unmoved.
Toward agreeable things,
My mind has no desire.
Toward things that disturb,
My mind is not disturbed.
My mind is thus developed —
From where can suffering come to me?

From: Theragāthā 2.36

item.title: “Monks, suppose there is urine mixed with various medicines. Then a person with jaundice comes, and someone says to him: ‘Good man, this urine is…
item.description:
“Monks, suppose there is urine mixed with various medicines. Then a person with jaundice comes, and someone says to him: ‘Good man, this urine is mixed with various medicines. If you wish, drink it. While drinking, you will not delight in its color, smell, or taste. But after drinking, you will be at ease.’ That person might drink it after reflection, without refusal. While drinking, he does not delight in its color, smell, or taste. But after drinking, he is at ease. Monks, I say that this course of practice is like that simile — namely, a course of practice that is painful in the present but has pleasant results in the future.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 46 – Mahādhammasamādānasutta

item.title: “Cut down the forest, not just a tree — From the forest, fear is born. Having cut down both forest and undergrowth, Be forest-free, O…
item.description:
“Cut down the forest, not just a tree —
From the forest, fear is born.
Having cut down both forest and undergrowth,
Be forest-free, O monks.”

“As long as even the smallest desire
Of a man for women is not cut off,
His mind is bound like a suckling calf to its mother.”

“Cut off your affection,
Like plucking an autumn lotus with the hand.
Develop the path to peace, Nibbāna,
Taught by the Well-gone One.”

From: Dhammapada 273-289

item.title: “Monks, form is suffering, both in the past and in the future, not to mention the present. Seeing this, monks, a well-taught noble disciple has…
item.description:
“Monks, form is suffering, both in the past and in the future, not to mention the present. Seeing this, monks, a well-taught noble disciple has no regret for past form, does not delight in future form, and practices disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation regarding present form. Feeling is suffering … Perception is suffering … Formations are suffering … Consciousness is suffering, both in the past and in the future, not to mention the present. Seeing this, monks, a well-taught noble disciple has no regret for past consciousness, does not delight in future consciousness, and practices disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation regarding present consciousness.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.10

item.title: “And, Carpenter, what is the practice that leads to the abandoning of unwholesome thoughts? Here, a monk awakens desire, makes effort, arouses energy, applies his…
item.description:
“And, Carpenter, what is the practice that leads to the abandoning of unwholesome thoughts? Here, a monk awakens desire, makes effort, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives so that unarisen evil, unwholesome states do not arise … so that arisen evil, unwholesome states are abandoned … so that unarisen wholesome states arise … so that arisen wholesome states are maintained, not confused, increased, expanded, developed, and fulfilled. Such is the practice that leads to the abandoning of unwholesome thoughts.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 78 – Samaṇamuṇḍikasutta

item.title: Stop, thoughts of sensual desire! Stop, thoughts of ill-will! Stop, thoughts of harmfulness! Enough, thoughts of sensual desire! Enough, thoughts of ill-will! Enough, thoughts of…
item.description:
Stop, thoughts of sensual desire!
Stop, thoughts of ill-will!
Stop, thoughts of harmfulness!
Enough, thoughts of sensual desire!
Enough, thoughts of ill-will!
Enough, thoughts of harmfulness!

From: Dīgha Nikāya 17 – Mahāsudassanasutta
